addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- integration-api-validator: Validates an external integration's API before any code is written. Characterizes transport, auth, pagination, response format, token refresh, and webhook style; identifies the closest existing integration as exemplar via parallel Explore searches. Use when starting a new integration via /plan-integration, or ad-hoc to re-characterize an existing integration whose source API has changed (vendor migration, new endpoints, deprecation). Outputs `.claude/references/{name}/api-summary.md`. (Tools: Bash, Read, Write, WebFetch, Grep, Glob)

- integration-data-seeder: Seeds a vendor's writes-safe sandbox with enough test data for downstream function-writer validation — products, inventory, orders distributed across states, returns, inbound shipments — and attempts state transitions (ship, cancel, process). Records under api-summary.md "Sandbox seeding" what was created and any state transitions that couldn't be driven via API (vendor UI required, real carrier needed, etc.). Spawned by the orchestrator after `integration-api-validator` finishes characterization, when the validator's reads turned up a thin or empty sandbox. Single-pass agent — runs once per integration build. (Tools: Bash, Read, Write, WebFetch, Grep, Glob)

- integration-function-writer: Implements one coherent unit of integration code — either a single data function (get_orders, get_inventory, write_order, etc.) or the auth bundle (get_integration_secret + <name>_request + validate_integration_secret). Iterates with yarn crawl + yarn test until validated. Standard path is via /plan-integration after the api-validator has produced api-summary.md. Can also be invoked ad-hoc for a single-method add to an existing integration when the exemplar is already known. Adheres strictly to .claude/references/integration-patterns.md. (Tools: Read, Edit, Write, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- integration-reviewer: Reviews a single unit of integration code (one data function, the auth bundle, or a single test file) against `.claude/references/integration-patterns.md`. Pattern-matches against the exemplar from api-summary.md when present. Runs targeted `yarn test`. Emits a structured BLOCK / APPROVE / APPROVE_WITH_NOTES verdict. Has no edit access — surfaces findings only. Use after each integration-function-writer invocation in /plan-integration, OR ad-hoc to review a single file or diff when debugging an integration, investigating a customer issue, or pre-PR. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- agent-pylon-investigate: Autonomous Pylon-ticket investigator for an unattended cloud routine. Fired once per new ticket by a Pylon webhook. Triage (skip noise / route non-technical / investigate) → check prior art → wrap the `investigate` skill → post a Pylon INTERNAL NOTE, and open a draft PR for a clear fix to the reported bug. Unrelated bugs found along the way go in the note, not a PR, and become a Linear card only when they would otherwise be lost. Fully unattended, internal-only. Use when handed a Pylon issue id (UUID) in a routine session.
- bulk-resync: Bulk resync connections for a given org and integration. Queries DynamoDB for connection IDs and runs the resync script.
- configure-schedule: Adjust crawl schedules for connections by modifying DynamoDB scheduler rows
- create-linear-issue: The one surface that creates a Linear issue. Two modes — compose a card from a freeform human ask (pick the Type label + integration/customer label, write a short human body), or file a caller-supplied spec from an automated skill like stale-schedule-investigate, which keeps the caller's title, labels and fenced blocks but trims its prose to the body ceiling and lands it in Robot Draft. Always reads the live workspace labels and statuses, and never invents a label. Use when asked to file/create/open a Linear issue, ticket, or card, and whenever another skill needs to create one. Out of scope: editing or closing existing issues.
- distill: Weekly consolidation pass over the .claude/ markdown — compact api-summary files to current API behavior, promote patterns humans taught via PR review into gotchas / rules / CLAUDE.md, and fix skill instructions whose output humans corrected on review. Use for the scheduled distillation routine or ad hoc when knowledge files have drifted into append-only history (`/distill [--lookback <days>]`). Markdown only: no code edits; the deliverable is a single draft PR.
- fan-out-change: Make one change ripple correctly across every integration (or every file in a large set) — a new canonical field, a renamed helper, a formatter-shape change, a signature migration. Use when a single schema/infra edit forces a matching edit in dozens or hundreds of `integrations/**/integration.py` files and each site needs per-integration judgment (real value vs IntegrationNotImplemented, docs-first surfacing, FOLLOW-UP when unverifiable) rather than a blind find-replace. Fan out by file/integration, each agent owning a slice; verify structurally before trusting any "done".
- fix-tests: Analyze failing tests from the daily CI report (Slack), a GitHub Actions run, or pasted yarn test output and implement root-cause fixes — both integration tests (live vendor crawls in test/integrations) and non-integration tests (api / celery / lambda / utils / transports). Use when asked to fix failing tests, work the daily CI failure report, or when given pytest failures. Every failure is reproduced and classified before any edit — never a green-at-any-cost shortcut like ignoring validation, weakening an assert, or skipping.
- integration-pr: Create or refresh a pokedex integration PR — body and field-mapping comment. Default behavior is create-from-current-branch; positional PR URL / `#NN` switches to refresh mode (detect-and-patch the existing body + mapping comment). Triggered by `/integration-pr [<pr>]`, or invoked via Skill() by `/wrap-integration` step 8 and `/plan-integration` finalize — the canonical PR-creation surface for orchestrating skills. Only for integration PRs — never invoke for a non-integration branch, and never auto-invoke from prose that merely mentions opening a PR.
- inventory-mapping: Build an inventory field-mapping breakdown — how each canonical Trackstar inventory field (awaiting/onhand/committed/unfulfillable/fulfillable/sellable) is derived from a given WMS integration's source fields. Use when a customer or ticket asks how Trackstar inventory fields map to the underlying integration.
- investigate: Investigate Trackstar integration issues — missing data, field mismatches, webhook failures, sync delays, stale schedules, crawl errors, credential problems, and customer-reported bugs. Use when debugging any connection issue, when a customer reports data problems, when schedules are stale, when analyzing Datadog error logs, or when triaging a support thread. Always use this skill for any Trackstar investigation, even if the issue type isn't immediately clear.
- pylon: Fetch Pylon issues, read messages, and post private (internal) notes via the Pylon REST API. Use when looking up a Pylon ticket by id, reading its message thread, or adding an internal note. Replaces the pylon MCP tools.
- query-datadog: How to query Datadog logs for Trackstar crawler investigations — the tags-vs-attributes distinction, the standard crawler log query for a connection / integration / function, pinning the time window to the staleness range, and building shareable Datadog links for PRs and Linear cards. Use whenever querying Datadog for a stale schedule, crawl error, sync issue, or any connection problem.
- review-code: Review integration code for quality, pattern adherence, and production readiness before merging
- review-dependabot-prs: Vet the open Dependabot bumps in pokedex and fold them into one of the existing Dependabot PRs, whose body becomes the evidence. Use when asked to review, triage, or clear the Dependabot queue, or when dependency-bump PRs have piled up. Each package is classified by blast radius and vetted against the code that actually uses it — a clean import and a green test run are not evidence for anything that fails silently in production. Opens the PR ready for a human; never merges it.
- run-scripts: Canonical invocations for the pokedex yarn scripts (yarn test, yarn crawl, yarn curl, yarn serve, yarn generate, yarn install-integration, yarn worker). Use whenever about to run tests, invoke pytest, exercise an integration method, scaffold a new integration, push dev credentials, or hit the local Pokedex API. **Required reading before running any tests** — never invoke `python -m pytest` or `pytest` directly; always use `yarn test` with the right filters.
- scrape-docs: Scrape and process API documentation from URLs, PDFs, or OpenAPI specs into LLM-optimized markdown
- se-investigate: Solutions-Engineer front door for a Pylon ticket. Triage (skip noise / route non-technical / investigate), check if we've already answered it (Slack + past Pylon tickets), run the investigation, then post findings as a Pylon INTERNAL NOTE. Use when handed a Pylon ticket id to investigate end-to-end. Runs unattended (a local poller opens a session per new ticket - see https://github.com/trackstarhq/pylon-dispatcher).
- stale-schedule-dispatch: Triage stale Trackstar crawl schedules and fan out one investigation per root-cause cluster. Use to run the stale-schedule dispatcher (scheduled routine or ad hoc) — pull the stale set, drop what shouldn't be worked on, dedup against in-flight investigations via the scheduler-row pointer, cluster by root cause, and fire one investigator per cluster. Read-only: no code edits, no PRs, no DynamoDB writes.
- stale-schedule-investigate: Diagnose the root cause of one stale Trackstar crawl-schedule cluster and either ship a tested fix as a PR or escalate with evidence. Use when handed a stale-schedule cluster (the dispatcher's /fire payload, or ad hoc) — investigate root cause, open the Linear issue, write the investigation pointer to the scheduler rows, then act per classification (code fix + PR, or escalate / customer / vendor / infra). Composes the read-only `investigate` skill for diagnosis.
- update-crawl-frequency: Update crawl_frequencies on a connection to change how often specific flows sync
- validate-api: Validate API behavior before implementation by testing auth, collecting samples, and documenting discrepancies
- catchup: Catchup - Review Branch Changes
- debug-report: Debug Report - Investigate Customer Issues
- diagram-trackstar: Regenerate the Trackstar architecture diagrams in docs/architecture/, grounded in real code
- generate-support-email: Generate Support Email - Draft Email to WMS/API Vendor
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

They're two different clocks on two different scopes, and both apply.

- `test/conftest.py:200` puts a `pytest.mark.timeout(60 * 4)` on the whole `test_install` test item. That's pytest-timeout killing the entire test — including the post-install work after the install call (auth-code row lookup, decrypt, and the secret-works verification that follows at `base_test.py:548+`).
- `base_test.py:543-548` sets a `SIGALRM` for 30s around **only** `integration.install(encoded_body)`. It's armed right before the call and cleared with `signal.alarm(0)` right after.

So the install call itself must return within 30s, while the whole test gets 240s. The narrower alarm fires first if an integration's install hangs, which gives you `TimeoutError("install test timeout 30s")` pointing straight at install rather than a generic 4-minute test timeout. Note the alarm skips the `requires_browser_install()` path, which returns earlier at line 540.

content.text:
`MAX_API_DURATION` is 60 (`config.py:58-59`). NetSuite's REST writes take 60-90s, so without the guard the conftest sweep would clamp them back to 60 and they'd fail. The guard lets a test file opt out of the blanket policy by declaring its own marker; the sweep only fills in a default where none was set.

`get_closest_marker` rather than a plain lookup because the override is at class level (`pytestmark`) while the marker being added is per-item, so it needs to walk up the node hierarchy to see it.

One incidental change worth knowing: the old `"auth" in item.nodeid` substring also caught three unrelated tests (`test_sanitized_request_bodies_redacts_basic_auth`, the two `test_install_resolve_reauth_*`) and marked them `auth`. They now fall to `no_perm_validator`, which matches what the marker is documented to mean. No run is affected, since `nonints` builds no `-m` expression.

.claude/skills/run-scripts/guides/test.md:210:`yarn test integrations -k <name> --perm` looks like it should narrow to one integration's perm validator tests. It doesn't. The `integrations` scope adds `test/integrations` as a collection root, and `-k <name>` resolves to `test/integrations/<type>/<name>/<name>_test.py`. Pytest then collects from BOTH paths and applies `-m 'perm'` to the combined set — running every integration's perm validator test.

content.text:
`no_perm` is the implicit "exclude the perm-validator tests" term. It's never selected by a flag; it's what `perm_str` falls back to whenever `--perm` is absent (`scripts/test.py:184-188`).

The subtlety is the guard at line 200: `if inttype_ops_resources_perm or perm_str == "perm"`. `no_perm` is only appended when the list already has something in it, i.e. when you narrowed by some *other* dimension (`--wms`, `--gets`, `--orders`, `--passthrough`, `--skip-retrieval`). So:

- **Narrowed by anything else** → `no_perm` is ANDed on, e.g. `-m '((wms) and (gets) and no_perm)'`. The perm tests are silently excluded so a `--gets` run doesn't also drag in the connection-less variants.
- **`--perm`** → `perm` is used instead, giving you only those tests.
- **No filter flags at all** → the list is empty and `perm_str == "no_perm"`, so nothing is appended, no `-m` is emitted, and everything runs, perm tests included.

That last branch is why a bare `yarn test -k deposco` runs all 52 items:

content.text:
Confirms it: no flags emits no `-m` at all, any other filter appends `and no_perm`, and `--perm` swaps to the positive term.

The practical effect is that the perm-validator tests are opt-in. They only run in a bare unfiltered sweep or when you explicitly pass `--perm` — every narrowed run excludes them. That's also why the marker has to be applied to *every* item in `conftest.py` rather than just the perm ones: `no_perm` is a real marker that the non-perm tests need to carry, not just the absence of `perm`.

content.text:
**900 seconds (15 minutes) in prod, 300 (5 min) everywhere else.** Set at `config.py:729`:

```python
"timeout": 15 * 60 if STAGE == "prod" else 5 * 60,
```

That single value drives three things:

- **The Lambda's own timeout** — CDK reads it in `templates/lambda_services.py` when building the function.
- **A soft in-handler budget of `timeout - 5`** (`lambda_handlers/permission_validator.py:21`), passed to `LambdaContextManager`, which arms a `SIGALRM` and raises `TimeoutError("execution timed out after 895s")` (`utils/lambda_util.py:32-34,66-67`). Same `signal.alarm` trick as the install test, and the point is to fire 5s before Lambda hard-kills the invocation so the handler can record the failure against the auth code instead of dying silently. Every lambda handler in the repo follows this `- 5` pattern.
- **The SQS visibility timeout, set to `timeout + 30`** (`templates/lambda_services.py:307`), so a message isn't redelivered while an invocation is still working on it.

Worth noting this is per SQS message, not per validated function: `batch_size` is 1 (`config.py:736`), so each message is one integration function getting its permissions checked, and each gets the full 15 minutes.

All the rename work is intact; you committed it as `ed72f9b41`/`0a73f1ea0` while I was working, so my remaining diff is just the timeout change (4 files).

**What I added.** A 30s `SIGALRM` around only the `get_function(...)` call at line 62 of `lambda_handlers/permission_validator.py`. On expiry it raises, logs, and marks the resource untested; everything else about the invocation proceeds normally.

The timeout is `PERMISSION_VALIDATOR_GET_TIMEOUT = 30` in `config.py:573`, per the constants-in-config rule.

Two things I had to handle that aren't obvious:

**The outer alarm.** `LambdaContextManager` already owns `SIGALRM` for the 895s invocation budget. A bare `signal.alarm(30)` would clobber it and `signal.alarm(0)` afterwards would cancel it outright, so a later hang would run to the hard Lambda kill with no error recorded. So the code captures what `signal.alarm()` returns (the outer alarm's remaining seconds), and in a `finally` restores it minus the time the get actually consumed.

**A dedicated exception rather than `TimeoutError`.** Since Python 3.10 `socket.timeout` *is* `TimeoutError`, so catching the builtin would report a slow vendor socket as our validator giving up. I added `PermissionValidationTimeout` in `utils/exceptions.py:161` and catch only that, ahead of the existing `PermissionsException` / generic handlers. A vendor socket timeout still falls through to the generic branch exactly as before.

One thing to confirm, since you said not to worry about the dynamo side: I set `failed_to_test = True` on timeout (the existing bucket for "couldn't determine permissions") and also added a `"timed_out"` key to `column_dict`. That last one writes a new column. Say the word and I'll drop it — `failed_to_test` alone is enough to keep it out of the blocked set.

message.content: any drawback to using time.time instead of time.monotonic?

content.text:
Yes, though the odds of it biting here are low.

`time.time()` is wall clock: NTP steps, manual clock sets, and leap-second smearing can move it forwards or backwards mid-measurement. `time.monotonic()` can't go backwards and ignores clock adjustments, which is exactly what you want for measuring a duration.

The consequence is specific to how the value gets used:

```python
get_elapsed = int(time.monotonic() - get_started_at)
signal.alarm(max(1, outer_remaining - get_elapsed))
```

A forward jump inflates `get_elapsed`, which drives `outer_remaining - get_elapsed` negative, the `max(1, ...)` clamps to 1, and the outer alarm fires a second later with `execution timed out after 895s` while 14 minutes of budget actually remained. A backward jump does the reverse: the restored alarm is set longer than the time really left, so the safety net misses and Lambda hard-kills the invocation with nothing recorded. Both are silent misattributions rather than crashes, which is the annoying kind to debug.

In practice Lambda runs on Amazon Time Sync and clock steps are rare, and a sandbox freeze happens between invocations rather than inside one, so you'd probably never see it. But monotonic is free and is the API meant for elapsed time, so there's no upside to switching.

One caveat worth knowing: `signal.alarm` is `ITIMER_REAL`, which counts real time on its own schedule, so the restore is approximate regardless of which clock you measure with. Monotonic just keeps your arithmetic from being the thing that's wrong.

Switched to `time.time()` at `lambda_handlers/permission_validator.py:74,105`. 9 passed.

Reasonable call, and it matches the closest analogue in the repo: `test/lambda/conftest.py:236-239` measures the mock Lambda context's elapsed time the same way. `time.monotonic()` only shows up in `transports/browser/backend.py`.

One small hardening you could add if you ever care about the clock-jump case, without leaving the `time.time()` pattern: clamp the elapsed to the window it can possibly occupy.

```python
get_elapsed = int(time.time() - get_started_at)
get_elapsed = min(max(get_elapsed, 0), PERMISSION_VALIDATOR_GET_TIMEOUT)
```

The get can't have run longer than its own alarm or for negative time, so that bounds the damage to the restored outer alarm regardless of what the wall clock does. Not necessary, just cheap. Happy to add it or leave as is.

content.text:
Mostly right, but there's one real bug and two things that don't do what they look like.

**1. `RetryException(10)` doesn't set the backoff.** The signature is `RetryException(message, retry_after_seconds=0, status_code=503)` (`utils/exceptions.py:36`), so `10` lands in `message`. `retry_after_seconds` stays 0, and `retry` sleeps `0 + 2 = 2` seconds, not 10. Worse, when all attempts are exhausted the test fails with an exception whose message is literally `10`, which tells the next reader nothing. You want:

```python
raise RetryException("permission validation get timed out", 10)
```

**2. `retry(3)` is 4 attempts, not 3.** The loop is `while wrap_retries >= 0` and only raises once the counter hits 0, so it's 1 initial try plus 3 retries (verified above). Fine if that's what you meant; use `retry(2)` for three total. Worst case with the fix in #1 is 4 × 20s + 3 × 12s = 116s, which still fits the 240s that `test/conftest.py:210` gives any `test_get` node.

**3. The `finally` cancels pytest's own test timeout.** This is the real bug. `pytest-timeout` implements the 240s budget with `SIGALRM` — I confirmed the pending alarm and its handler above. So `signal.alarm(20)` overwrites it, and `signal.alarm(0)` in the `finally` cancels it outright. From the first attempt onward, the test has no timeout guard at all; if the vendor then hangs somewhere outside the alarmed block, it hangs until CI kills the whole job rather than failing at 240s.

It's the same problem I handled in the lambda handler, so mirror that fix: capture what `signal.alarm()` returns and put it back.

```python
@retry(3)
def do_get_with_timeout():
    outer_handler = signal.signal(signal.SIGALRM, raise_get_timeout)
    outer_remaining = signal.alarm(20)
    started_at = time.time()
    try:
        rsp = get_function(start_time, end_time, first_crawl, first_loop)
    except PermissionValidationTimeout:
        raise RetryException("permission validation get timed out", 10)
    finally:
        signal.alarm(0)
        signal.signal(signal.SIGALRM, outer_handler)
        if outer_remaining:
            elapsed = int(time.time() - started_at)
            signal.alarm(max(1, outer_remaining - elapsed))
    return rsp
```

That needs `import time` in `base_test.py` (`signal` is already imported at line 6).

Two smaller notes. `test_install` at `base_test.py:543-548` already has this same clobbering pattern, so it's pre-existing in the repo, but the retry loop makes it bite harder here since the alarm is destroyed on the first attempt and every later attempt runs unguarded. And the bound is hardcoded `20` while the lambda reads `PERMISSION_VALIDATOR_GET_TIMEOUT` from config; since the comment above it says "copied from permission_validator", the two will drift. Given the repo rule about constants living in `config.py`, a `PERMISSION_VALIDATOR_TEST_GET_TIMEOUT = 20` would keep that honest.

Applied to both, no config change.

**`get_with_perm_validator`** (`base_test.py:922-939`) — fixed the `RetryException` args so the 10s backoff actually takes effect and the exhausted-retries failure carries a readable message instead of `10`, and the `finally` now saves and restores pytest's alarm.

**`test_install`** (`base_test.py:551-562`) — same save/restore, and the install call is now wrapped in `try/finally` so the alarm gets cleaned up when install raises. Previously a failing install left the 30s alarm armed, which would fire later during the auth-code assertions and report an unrelated "install test timeout 30s".

Added `import time` at `base_test.py:7`. Left `retry(3)` alone since 4 total attempts looked deliberate; worst case is now 4 × 20s plus 3 × 12s of backoff = 116s, inside the 240s that `test/conftest.py:210` gives `test_get` nodes.

Verified the mechanism directly rather than by eye. The old pattern leaves `remaining=0` with the test's handler replaced, i.e. the 240s budget is gone. The new one leaves pytest-timeout's handler in place with `remaining=30` after a clean block, and `remaining=27` after three consecutive 1s inner timeouts, so the retry loop debits the outer budget by exactly what it consumed.

I didn't run the perm-validator tests themselves; they're live vendor crawls and the alarm path only triggers against a hanging vendor.

Rebase is done, all 11 commits applied onto `0aa2b43c4`, working tree clean, 9545 tests collect. (Those lines are just test names containing "error", not failures.)

Three conflicts, all the same underlying cause: upstream `main` added `integration.crawl_scope(resource)` around the get call in both the validator and its base test, and your commits were editing the same lines.

**`lambda_handlers/permission_validator.py`** — kept the `crawl_scope` wrapper inside the alarmed `try` and the `except PermissionValidationTimeout` branch alongside the other handlers. Both sides were additive.

**`integrations/wms/skuvault/integration.py`** — upstream added `shipment_parcels.extend(...)` inside the shipment loop plus a post-loop kit lookup; your commit added `if self.in_perm_validator(): break`. Put the `break` at the end of the chunk loop body so the new post-loop block still runs, just over the one chunk the validator fetched.

**`test/integrations/base_test.py`** — mirrored the lambda resolution: `crawl_scope` moved inside `do_get_with_timeout`, so it's under the 20s alarm, and the outer `try` calls the retrying wrapper.

Two things worth knowing about the merged result:

The alarm is armed *before* `crawl_scope.__enter__`, so for browser carriers the 30s budget now covers browser session setup and login, not just the get. That's the behavior I'd want (the whole operation is bounded), but it means a slow portal login can trip the timeout where it previously wouldn't. In the base test it's moot, since upstream also added a `uses_browserbase()` skip just above.

And with the retry loop, `crawl_scope` is entered and exited per attempt, so a retry gets a fresh session rather than reusing a dead one.

I only ran the lambda tests (9 passed) and full collection. The skuvault and perm-validator integration tests are live vendor crawls, so I left those to you.

commit dbfd572d05091b6d80b46a98324d212a457bfc86
Author: DanielLanger <dlanger99@gmail.com>
Date:   Wed Sep 9 17:15:30 2026 -0400

    Fix five crawls that were failing in prod (#5976)
    
    * fulfillor: report an unreachable host as invalid credentials
    
    Cin7's connection has been failing every crawl with a ConnectTimeout to
    health3pl-admin.fulfillor.com. The host resolves but never completes a TCP
    connect, while fulfillor.com itself is up, so it is that 3PL's server or an
    IP block rather than a vendor outage.
    
    Each 3PL runs its own Fulfillor server behind a customer-supplied api_url, so
    there is nothing on our side to retry. Surface it as invalid credentials so
    the customer sees a connection error they can act on instead of the crawl
    failing silently every cycle.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01NdSJXasnVGaBvKEjqJe1Kk
    
    * fulfillor: cap the connect timeout; etsy: classify failed token refresh
    
    Fulfillor requests had no connect timeout, so five urllib3 retries against an
    unreachable host held a crawl worker for about ten minutes before failing. Cap
    the connect at 10s and leave the read uncapped, since a slow list endpoint is
    not a connection problem.
    
    Etsy's token refresh read response.json() without checking the status, so a
    429 or a rejected refresh surfaced as a JSON decode error. Raise a throttle on
    429 (honouring Retry-After) and invalid credentials otherwise.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01NdSJXasnVGaBvKEjqJe1Kk
    
    * etsy: exempt the token refresh from the throttle-retry check
    
    refresh_etsy_creds raises a throttle outside an @retry function. The crawl path
    calls it from inside etsy_request's wrapped inner, which already retries, and
    wrapping the refresh itself would sleep out Etsy's multi-hour daily-limit
    Retry-After and stall the crawl. Same shape as the linnworks exemption.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01NdSJXasnVGaBvKEjqJe1Kk
    
    * address review: narrow both classifications
    
    fulfillor: catch ConnectTimeout rather than the whole ConnectionError
    hierarchy. SSLError and ProxyError are subclasses and are our side, not a dead
    tenant host. Re-verified against the still-blocked host: still classified,
    still 63s.
    
    etsy: a 5xx from the token endpoint is Etsy having a bad day, not a dead
    refresh token, so it fails the crawl and retries next cycle instead of telling
    the customer to reconnect.
    
    api-summary: the host times out (silent SYN drop), it does not refuse. Cite
    TRA-2724 and the control connection that isolates this to one tenant.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit b5d07d262e5d7b0692c5aec25b0839a6ed915342
Author: trackstardev <99369259+trackstardev@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Wed Sep 9 17:05:45 2026 -0400

    [TRA-2876] helm-wms: read supplier links from the inventory list to unblock get_products (#5963)
    
    * [TRA-2876] helm-wms: read supplier links from the inventory list
    
    get_products has aborted on every crawl since 2026-09-03 with
    KeyError: 'inventory_suppliers'. Helm renamed the product-supplier join
    to supplier_links and changed the row shape, and none of the three
    production sites returns the old name on any endpoint any more.
    
    The new field also comes back on GET /inventory itself, alongside every
    other field format_product reads, so the per-item GET /inventory/{id}
    call is gone. That was one extra request per product (39 on the largest
    connection, each with its own login), and it is what made a single 500
    on one record kill the whole page (TRA-2680).
    
    Field mapping, checked live: supplier_links[].contact_id is the supplier
    and matches the id GET /suppliers returns for the same name, which is the
    id create_inbound_shipment posts back; the row's own id is the join
    record, so it becomes external_id. supplier_name replaces shipping_name.
    cost_price fills unit_cost, which was IntegrationNotImplemented while the
    vendor was in fact sending it. primary_supplier now picks supplier_object,
    falling back to a lone link since some sites never tick the flag.
    
    Our test site is on an older Helm build that sends no supplier_links on
    any endpoint, so the read tolerates the field being absent.
    
    Verified: yarn test -k helm-wms (22 passed, 28 skipped) and a clean
    yarn crawl -s prod --max-pages 3 on all three production connections
    from the page that was failing.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01HZttp9CbpZd3veo4L21FWM
    
    * helm-wms: shorten the supplier_links comment to two lines
    
    Greptile flagged it against the two-line ceiling in code-style.md.
    Comment only, no behaviour change.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01HZttp9CbpZd3veo4L21FWM
    
    * helm-wms: record the supplier_links mapping decisions (TRA-2876)
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01HZu5nJjwHNgbujmw8S3ZYm
    
    ---------
    
    Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

content.text:
Upstream deliberately removed that per-item `GET /inventory/{id}` call in PR #5963: Helm now returns `supplier_links` on the list endpoint, and the N+1 was killing whole pages on a single 500. My commit's side would resurrect it, and would also break, since the line below the conflict now reads `response["last_page"]` while my side named the variable `list_response`.

Taking upstream's version here:

Your "couple more" commit capped `get_products` to one item under `in_perm_validator()` to avoid the per-item `GET /inventory/{id}` fetch. Upstream PR #5963 (TRA-2876) deleted that fetch entirely: Helm now returns `supplier_links` on the list endpoint, so the N+1 is gone, and it was what let a single 500 kill a whole page. I took upstream's version and dropped your hunk, because the cap now saves nothing (there's no per-item request left, just local formatting), and because your side would have broken outright: the line below the conflict now reads `response["last_page"]` while your side named the variable `list_response`, which is a `NameError` on every call.

def get_orders_from_edge(self, start):
        customer_id = self.edge_customer_id()
        # the window filters on the planned ship date, not on when anything last
        # changed, so it has to reach into the future to see orders not yet sent
        window_end = now() + timedelta(days=EDGE_ORDER_LOOKAHEAD_DAYS)
        orders = self.edge_request(
            "api/Orders",
            params={
                "startDate": start.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"),
                "endDate": window_end.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"),
                "customerId": customer_id,
                "orderType": EDGE_OUTBOUND_ORDER_TYPE,
            },
        )
        orders += self.edge_in_flight_orders(customer_id, window_end)

        # an order sent out in more than one load is several rows here, one per
        # load, all carrying the same po number
        loads_by_po = {}
        po_sequence = []
        unreadable_po_numbers = []
        seen_order_numbers = []
        for order in orders:
            # edge ignores an orderType it does not recognise and returns
            # everything, so check rather than trust the filter alone
            if order["orderType"] != EDGE_OUTBOUND_ORDER_TYPE:
                continue
            # an order due to go out soon answers both reads above
            if order["orderNumber"] in seen_order_numbers:
                continue
            seen_order_numbers.append(order["orderNumber"])
            po_number = order["poNumber"]
            if po_number not in loads_by_po:
                loads_by_po[po_number] = []
                po_sequence.append(po_number)
            order_number = order["orderNumber"]
            business_system = order["orderNumberBusinessSystem"]
            # the carrier, the bill of lading and the date the order was placed
            # are only on the single-order call
            try:
                detail = self.edge_request(
                    f"api/Orders/{order_number}", params={"bsid": business_system}
                )
                commodities = self.edge_request(
                    f"api/Orders/{order_number}/commodities",
                    params={"bsid": business_system},
                )
            except PokedexException as e:
                # a handful of orders belong to a part of rjw this login cannot
                # see, and without their lines there is no order to build. record
                # it against the connection rather than losing every other order
                if e.status_code != EDGE_NO_ACCESS_STATUS:
                    raise
                api_call_path = f"edge order {order_number}"
                self.api_call_errors[api_call_path] = self.create_permissions_exception(
                    api_call_path
                )
                # its quantities count towards the po's totals and its status, so
                # writing the po without it would understate what was ordered and
                # could call a half shipped order complete
                if po_number not in unreadable_po_numbers:
                    unreadable_po_numbers.append(po_number)
                continue
            loads_by_po[po_number].append((order, detail, commodities))

        # a load sent before this window is not in the response at all, and
        # writing the order would drop it, so read back everything we already
        # hold. the load still in the window may not have gone out yet, so this
        # cannot be limited to orders that look shipped right now
        existing_by_id = {}

Nothing staged. Answering your question first, since the two parts differ:

**Inbounds: yes, it needs the same guard.** `get_inbound_shipments_from_edge` calls `api/Orders/{order_number}/commodities` per delivery — the exact endpoint `get_orders_from_edge` already wraps. A delivery belonging to a part of rjw the login can't see returns 403, `edge_request` raises `PokedexException` (`rjw/integration.py:465`), and today it propagates out of the whole function, losing every other inbound. Same failure orders was hardened against.

I mirrored the orders treatment rather than just swallowing it: record the permissions exception under `edge inbound {order_number}`, then skip the whole PO. Several deliveries roll into one PO and `format_inbound_shipment_from_edge` adds their quantities up, so emitting a PO with one delivery missing would report less arrived than did — the same reasoning behind `unreadable_po_numbers` in orders.

**Inventory: no.** `get_inventory_from_edge` only touches `api/Dashboards/Inventory/inventory-summary` and `.../{sku}/lots`, both scoped by `customerId`. The 403 is specifically about an *order* under a part of rjw the login can't see (`EDGE_NO_ACCESS_STATUS` comment at line 118); there's no per-order resource in the inventory path, so a try/except there would be guarding a failure that can't happen. I left it alone.

**Early return** added to both `get_inventory:604` and `get_inbound_shipments:696`, on the non-edge branch only. The EDI path is sftp plus s3 and can't refuse a read, so there's nothing for the validator to find — and `crawl_server()` would blow the 30s alarm anyway. The edge branch above it still runs, since that's where permission errors actually come from.

Two things worth your call. `get_orders:795` has the identical non-edge EDI path and the same argument applies, but you only named inventory and inbounds so I left it. And the early return omits `file_to_archive`, which the normal path includes; that's fine because nothing consumes the response in validator mode, but it does mean the two branches return different shapes.

Not staged, not committed. I haven't run the rjw tests — they're live vendor crawls, and the 403 branch needs a delivery the test login can't see.
